passage:
I share a flat with Mohit, so I noticed the phone calls. Mohit's college friend had started giving nearly all savings and every weekend to a group. Mohit never lectured. Every Thursday Mohit rang: "How was your week? What's the best part? How do you decide how much to give?"

Once the friend hung up sharply. Mohit just sent a silly picture and, "Still on for dosa on Saturday?"

I'm Sudha, and I told Mohit to say plainly that it was a trap. Mohit shook a head. "If I attack the group, I lose my friend. Then who do they call when doubts come?"

Last week the friend rang at midnight, voice shaky. "Can I ask you something?"

I can't tell how worried Mohit is inside. I only saw Mohit's face when the phone lit up.

qa.q: How often did Mohit ring the friend?
Why did Mohit choose not to attack the group?
qa.a: Mohit feared losing the friend: if the group were attacked, the friend might not call Mohit when doubts arrived.
More open questions about what the group asks for and how the friend decides how much to give, while staying warm and keeping plans like the dosa on Saturday.

qa.q: How does Sudha see Mohit's approach?
qa.a: Sudha first wanted Mohit to say plainly that it was a trap, but the midnight call from the friend shows why staying in touch mattered.

grounding: Mohit worries about a friend giving all savings and time to a group, stays warm, asks open questions and keeps the friendship alive.
